doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Advice to young musicians: pick a hero and do the research
summary: Young players have more resources than he did; he advises picking a hero, researching styles, and mentions Radio Farm and Richard Tee's homework line.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Oh. What do you think of the progression of the music business since — well this is a very large question but you got started in the 70s and as you said there was all kinds of work. What do you think a young musician now faces and any advice for them?

Well in my mind and in my ears the young musician today has so many more advantages than I had in terms of what’s available for research purposes between YouTube and all the recordings and all the different formats and all the different places they can see somebody that they want to emulate, or listen to something, download it, stream it, and practice with it 24 hours a day to get that feel, and I hear a lot of good young drummers who have done exactly that: downloaded the records, a lot of them, especially the hip hop stuff you know made with a drum machine, it’s got these impossible beats because they’re all programmed but the young drummer takes it at face value. You know this is © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

what’s on the record, this is what I’ve got to play, and I’ve got to figure out a way to get that sound you know whether it means tuning the snare drum way, way high and putting a pot lid on it so it’s got this metallic backbeat to it, metallic sound, or putting a piece of construction material on it like these aluminum 2 X 4 sections that they use instead of 2 X 4s these days. You compress that and it’s a great metallic snare drum sound. I’ve used that a couple of times. And ridiculous little tiny electronic hi-hat parts, you know where they’re playing 64th notes — again. But the young drummer today says, “All right, that’s what I gotta do.” You know the same way I did from listening to music of the 60s and 70s, emulating whatever I heard on the record, figure out how they did it, how does Jake Hanna get that sound with Woody Herman? You know is it the size of the ride cymbal or how does Ronnie Zito — getting that sound with Woody Herman. Is the snare drum wide open? Are they 15 inch hi-hats? Is it a 22 inch ride cymbal? Whatever it was, and listen to the record over and over and over again until I sound like him. So the advice I would give is the same as I’ve always given no matter what, whether it’s 2023 or 1970 you know pick out a hero, pick out somebody you really want to emulate or a couple of guys you really want to emulate. Whether it’s Bernard Purdie or Al Jackson or Roger Hawkins or Steve Gadd of course or Steve Jordan or Steve Ferroni.

Well, pick out that person and do the research. Do the homework as Richard Tee would say, “Do the homework, Stuffy.” And really make yourself a musicologist in terms of style and all the different kinds of music that are out there now, my God, every single country has got its own indigenous music in the world. And oh there’s a great site called Radio Farm, you can google it and it’s got a world map with all these little green dots on it and you can go anywhere on the world map and click on one of these green dots and get the radio station from that country. And I go a lot to West Africa or Cuba or Jamaica. There’s none — you can’t get any radio stations from Russia or China. But everywhere else, you can get all the Japanese radio stations, you can get radio stations in Bulgaria and listen to Bulgarian shepherd music. So there’s all kinds of resources that I didn’t have when I was trying to do that. But the same basic principles still apply, you know pick out a hero, pick out somebody you want to emulate and do the research you know. Really learn about a certain musical style or learn about what that particular guy or girl, whether it’s a drummer or a horn player or a singer, you know really find out what makes them tick and how they got to where they got, who they studied with or who they didn’t study with. That really works for me, it has worked for me in terms of learning all different kinds of music, whether I’m the best Latin player or whether I’m the best Brazilian player, you know it doesn’t really matter. It’s a question of being aware of that music and be willing to emulate it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
